topic.subject: social
topic.title: Media and advertising
topic.scope: media and technology, money and media, balanced reporting, advertising, brands, democracy

misconceptions.statement: If a news channel is independent, it must be telling the absolute truth.
misconceptions.why: Students conflate 'independent from government' with 'objective and unbiased'.
misconceptions.fix: Independent media is free from government control but can still be biased due to corporate interests or editorial choices.

probe.question: Can a private newspaper be biased?
probe.wrong_answer: No, only government-run media is biased.

misconceptions.statement: Advertisements are only meant to inform us about new products.
misconceptions.why: Students focus on the explicit content of the ad rather than the underlying persuasive intent.
misconceptions.fix: Advertisements are designed to persuade consumers to buy products by creating a desire or associating the product with a lifestyle.

probe.question: Why do companies spend money on ads?
probe.wrong_answer: To tell people what products are available.

misconceptions.root_belief: Information is the only purpose of communication.

misconceptions.statement: The media tells us what is important, so we should believe everything they highlight.
misconceptions.why: Students assume that the frequency of news coverage equals the objective importance of an event.
misconceptions.fix: Media sets the agenda by choosing which stories to highlight, but this does not mean those are the only important issues.

probe.question: If the news talks about a celebrity all day, is it the most important event in the country?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because the news says it is.

misconceptions.statement: Expensive brands are always better quality than cheaper, unbranded goods.
misconceptions.why: Students internalize the messaging of advertisements that equate price with quality.
misconceptions.fix: Advertising creates a brand image that makes products seem superior, but the actual quality may be the same as unbranded items.

probe.question: Is a branded shirt always better than a local one?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because the brand is famous.

misconceptions.statement: Newspapers and TV channels earn all their money from people buying them, not from advertisements.
misconceptions.why: Students see the copy price or cable bill and do not notice that ads pay most production costs.
misconceptions.fix: Media houses earn a large part of their income from advertisements. Sale price alone does not cover the cost, so ads fund media and keep it cheap.

probe.question: A newspaper costs only Rs 5 but is expensive to print. Where does most of the extra money come from?
probe.wrong_answer: From readers paying more money for each copy.

misconceptions.root_belief: Consumers alone pay for all media costs
misconceptions.source_hint: NCERT Class 7 Social Science textbook; classroom observation

misconceptions.statement: Media is free for us, so it costs nothing to run a TV channel or newspaper.
misconceptions.why: Students watch TV or read free websites without paying and assume there are no costs.
misconceptions.fix: Running media needs money for reporters, equipment, printing, broadcasting and salaries. Someone, often advertisers, pays for these.

probe.question: Why does a free TV channel still need money?
probe.wrong_answer: It does not need money because viewers watch it free.

misconceptions.root_belief: Free to the viewer means free to produce

misconceptions.statement: Technology only changed how media looks, not who can reach or use it.
misconceptions.why: Students see new gadgets as better screens and not as a change in access and speed.
misconceptions.fix: New technology such as printing, radio, TV and the internet changed how fast news spreads and how many people can share or receive it.

probe.question: How did the internet change media compared with early newspapers?
probe.wrong_answer: It only made pictures look better; nothing else changed.

misconceptions.root_belief: Technology changes only appearance, not reach

misconceptions.statement: Mass media means only television and nothing else reaches millions.
misconceptions.why: TV is the most familiar medium at home, so students equate it with mass media.
misconceptions.fix: Mass media includes newspapers, radio, TV, films and the internet. All of them reach very large numbers of people.

probe.question: Which of these are mass media: newspaper, radio, TV, internet?

misconceptions.statement: If I like a brand's advertisement, I should buy that brand because the ad proves it is the best.
misconceptions.why: Students treat an appealing ad, jingle or celebrity as evidence of product quality.
misconceptions.fix: Ads aim to make people like and stay loyal to a brand, but they do not prove quality. We should compare price, quality and need before buying.

probe.question: A popular actor appears in a biscuit ad you love. What does this show about the biscuit?
probe.wrong_answer: It shows the biscuit must be the best quality.

misconceptions.source_hint: media literacy research on children and advertising

misconceptions.statement: Advertisements affect only adults, so children are not influenced by them.
misconceptions.why: Students think buying decisions belong only to those who earn money.
misconceptions.fix: Ads target children too, and children influence what families buy, such as snacks, toys and clothes.

probe.question: Why do companies make colourful ads with cartoons during children's shows?
probe.wrong_answer: Children cannot be influenced, so it is only for decoration.

misconceptions.root_belief: Only earners are influenced by advertising
misconceptions.source_hint: research on children's awareness of advertising intent

misconceptions.statement: Balanced reporting means giving equal time to every opinion, even a false one.
misconceptions.why: Students link balance with fairness in counting, not with checking facts.
misconceptions.fix: Balanced reporting presents different sides fairly and accurately, based on facts, and does not treat falsehood as equal to evidence.

probe.question: A channel gives the same airtime to a proven fact and a rumour. Is this balanced reporting?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, equal time to both makes it balanced.

misconceptions.root_belief: Balance means equal time regardless of facts

misconceptions.statement: In a democracy, media should always support the government.
misconceptions.why: Students confuse respect for government with the media's duty to inform.
misconceptions.fix: In a democracy, media should report on government work, including its mistakes, so citizens can question and make informed choices.

probe.question: A newspaper reports a mistake in a government scheme. What should the media have done?
probe.wrong_answer: It should have stayed quiet and supported the government.

misconceptions.root_belief: Good media must agree with the government
misconceptions.source_hint: NCERT Class 7 Social Science textbook; civics teaching
